item.title: Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo
item.description:
Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A member of the executive on Oldebroek council in Gelderland has apologised for posting a photograph of himself posing with a Kalashnikov in front of a pro-Russian flag. Standing next to him in the photo is a former Almere council candidate for the far-right FvD party, according to the Volkskrant.

Tom de Nooijer, of the local Christelijk Verbond Oldebroek party, shared the image on Instagram after visiting Transnistria, a self-declared, unrecognised pro-Russian region that broke away from Moldova after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

De Nooijer said he had been on holiday in Moldova and travelled to the region out of a “historical interest in the Soviet past”, and went to a shooting range there. He said the trip was private and not meant as a political statement. He is a former presenter of the right-wing broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland.

He initially declined to comment or apologise, prompting anger from opposition councillors. “They fled the violence he is glorifying by posing for a pro-Russian flag,” said Frank van ’t Ende, referring to the 200 Ukrainian refugees the council houses. A ChristenUnie councillor called the photo “shocking”.

Mayor Tanja Haseloop-Amsing told Omroep Gelderland that the council’s executive had been “unpleasantly surprised” by the image.

In a written statement on Wednesday, De Nooijer distanced himself from the hammer-and-sickle flag in the photo, called the visit unwise and apologised to anyone who might have been insulted.

item.title: Dutch spy agencies to get more powers against foreign enemies
item.description:
Dutch spy agencies to get more powers against foreign enemies

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands’ two intelligence agencies are to gain new powers to track and disrupt “obvious adversaries” such as Russian hackers, Chinese spies and Iranian operatives without asking permission in advance, under a draft law published by the cabinet.

The domestic intelligence service AIVD and military intelligence service MIVD would no longer need prior sign-off to follow an individual hacker online. “By then they have already gone,” said defence minister Dilan Yesilgöz.

Once a foreign service is formally designated an adversary, the agencies could pursue anyone thought to be working for it, with a watchdog checking afterwards whether their actions were lawful and able to halt operations it considers inappropriate.

The plans have raised concerns about the privacy of Dutch citizens. Yesilgöz said oversight would remain in place. “Putin and his cronies do not deserve our privacy, but the people of the Netherlands do,” she said.

The bill would also let the agencies work more closely with Dutch banks, universities and online platforms, warn them of risks and, in some cases, demand information from them. Interior minister Pieter Heerma, who is responsible for the AIVD, declined to name specific organisations.

It follows the previous cabinet’s abandoned plan to screen 8,000 foreign researchers and students for espionage risks, which was judged unworkable. Oversight of the two agencies would be merged into a single body.

The draft is open for public consultation before it goes to parliament.

item.title: “We have to stop this man”: mass sperm donor fathered 121 kids
item.description:
“We have to stop this man”: mass sperm donor fathered 121 kids

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch man has fathered at least 121 children as a sperm donor and is still active, according to an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur – the latest in a line of mass donors who exploit a gap in the legal rules by working outside licensed clinics.

The man, who is 43 and from the Groningen region, donated to several sperm banks but operates mainly online, approaching women directly. Investigators spoke to dozens of affected mothers, and said the true figure is probably far higher.

They also found that the man sat on a government commission that evaluated the Dutch donor law in 2019. It is unclear how or why he was appointed.

Dutch clinics may not use a single donor for more than 12 families. But donors and would-be parents who arrange conception privately are bound by no legal maximum, a gap that lets a determined donor father dozens or hundreds of children unchecked. Nieuwsuur revealed last year that clinics had produced at least 85 mass donors.

The health and youth care inspectorate IGJ, part of the health ministry, said it did not know the man and called the case “very undesirable”. But a spokesperson said the inspectorate oversees care provided in clinics, not conception arranged in the private sphere.

Evasive behaviour 
The donor children’s foundation Stichting Donorkind and several of the mothers want him to stop. “We have to stop this man,” they told the programme.

The mothers say he lies about how many children he has fathered, growing evasive or hinting he will break off contact when pressed – leverage that matters to women who want their child to be able to know their biological father one day.

Some of the women told Nieuwsuur he sent them sexually suggestive messages, offering to help conceive via the “natural method.” One mother from the Randstad who tried to report him said the police were no help. “The police just stared at me blankly,” she said.

Traces abroad
There are also signs that the same man has fathered children abroad. One mother traced several children in Germany through an online DNA database, and the man has donated at a Danish sperm bank.

The man declined to be interviewed, saying he wanted any contact to run anonymously through the mothers or official bodies. He asked for privacy for himself and the families, and would not confirm how many children he has conceived.

The most notorious Dutch case remains that of Jonathan Meijer, who fathered some 550 children worldwide and was ordered by a court to stop in 2023.

item.title: Majority of student rooms priced well over the legal limit
item.description:
Majority of student rooms priced well over the legal limit

August 28, 2026 Louis Gore-Langton

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The majority of student rooms on the Netherlands’ biggest rental platform, Kamernet, are being advertised at prices well over the legal limit – an average of €239 a month, and more than €400 in Amsterdam – investigative outlet Argos has found. Local councils are not intervening and say they have no power to do so.

Argos compared rent on 2,637 ads against the maximum each room is legally allowed to charge. Six in ten rooms were priced above the legal maximum over July and August, with landlords of overpriced rooms asking an average of €239 a month more than the rules permit.

In some cities, like Amsterdam, where the average room costs nearly €1,000 a month, 97% of the rooms Argos sampled were above the cap, by an average of €421 a month. In Utrecht the figure was 72%.

Utrecht and Nijmegen issued no fines and lowered no rents last year, while Rotterdam and The Hague were the exceptions, acting far more often.

Amsterdam council reaction
Since the Affordable Rent Act 2025 was introduced, which caps prices by a points system based on a room’s size and features, councils have been required to intervene – something the investigation found is not being done in many cities.

A spokesperson for Amsterdam council housing executive Zita Pels told DutchNews that the council cannot take legal action on advertising alone – an illegal rent must already be in force before it can do something. So students must first get into an illegally high rental contract before they can be helped.

The spokesperson also said the council “strongly opposes” the way people “shamelessly” exploit the housing crisis in Amsterdam, but that it unfortunately cannot do more about the advertising problem.

They also said the council itself advertises on rental platforms, attends student events, and visits tenants at home, because many people are reluctant to report overcharging for fear of losing their room.

In March, Amsterdam council also imposed a €45,000 penalty on the manager of a student complex in Amsterdam’s Zuidoost district for a range of violations, the council highlighted, including excessive rents. The landlord can still object.

There is a tenant advice foundation called !Woon that the council subsidises. Its 2025 report records more than 19,000 contacts about rent or service charges and 575 reports of serious landlord misconduct, and lists cases it has won, including 21 rulings against a single landlord, one of which cut a rent from €1,076 to €280.

The council’s own enforcement report to councillors, published in May, shows direct action on rents is a small part of the picture. Of 726 complaints under the new rental laws in 2025, 96 concerned rent levels; 167 were passed to !Woon and 102 fell outside the rules. The bulk of the council’s 1,836 enforcement outcomes last year involved empty or misused homes, not overcharging.

Code yellow issued for thunderstorms this afternoon

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch weather service KNMI has issued a code yellow alert for heavy thunderstorms expected in the country this afternoon.

With the thunder, wind gusts of 60-75 km/h, 2cm balls of hail and heavy rain over a short period are possible. KNMI also says to watch out for downed tree branches and local flooding. Traffic could also be affected.

The thunderstorms will move from the southwest to the northeast of the country and are expected to be over by early evening.

item.title: It ain’t pretty: botched Botox on the rise in country’s youth
item.description:
It ain’t pretty: botched Botox on the rise in country’s youth

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Just as the new school year gets underway, the Dutch Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) has warned about a five-fold increase in complaints resulting from failed cosmetic treatments involving Botox and other dermal fillers.

The IGC received 175 reports of failed treatments, up from some 35 per year in the preceding years. The skyrocketing numbers, they say, are largely due to increased demand for the procedures among youth looking for fuller lips and less wrinkles and a surge in places providing them.

Young people, IGJ inspector Rosemarie Jansen told broadcaster NOS, were especially vulnerable to cutthroat rates among providers who often lack the mandatory qualifications to provide them. That “lowers the threshold for young people, precisely because they do not have much to spend,” she said.

Some 67% of the complaints involved a practitioner who was not legally qualified or lacked the necessary medical competence.

In the Netherlands, a doctor is required to be present when a patient receives such cosmetic treatments, something which is lacking in the proliferation of places offering them.

The botched procedures have led to swelling and drooping eyelids, lip inflammation and allergic reactions. The ICJ says the number of complaints is likely unreported due to the shame many young people feel about getting cosmetic work.

Fillercheck.nl

To help combat the problem, the IGC, along with Tilburg University and the consumer platform wiemooiwilzijn, have created fillercheck.nl, a website where those seeking cosmetic treatments can go down a four-part checklist that gets them thinking about the treatment, lets them find out if their provider is qualified and, says the IGC, help them recognize red flags.

The Inspectorate is taking their message via pop-up clinics disguised as cosmetic treatment centres to students in Amsterdam, Nijmegen, Zwolle and Breda this week and next – just in time for university introduction weeks.

item.title: More deposit bottles returned but still short of legal mandate
item.description:
More deposit bottles returned but still short of legal mandate

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Although more people are returning their cans and bottles for recycling and cash back, the mandatory collection target of 90% is not being met, just as it hasn’t since the deposit scheme was first introduced five years ago.

According to Verpact, the foundation that oversees the statiegeld (deposit) system in the Netherlands, based on figures from the first half of the year, 78% of deposit bottles will be collected in 2026; for cans, that number jumps to 86%.

Since 2021, when the deposit scheme for bottles and cans was first introduced, producers and importers have been required by law to collect and recycle 90% of plastic bottles and cans.

While the percentages have been increasing – last year 77% of plastic bottles and 83% of cans were returned – the 90% target is unlikely to be reached again this year, according to Verpact’s preliminary 2025 annual report.

“We cannot continue doing what we have always done and expect to continue meeting our statutory targets in the future,” said Hester Klein Lankhorst, Verpact’s chair of the executive board, of the changing European landscape.

She said companies currently not taking a deposit should be obliged to and calls for more recycling capacity in Europe. She sees a ban on selling cans and bottles without deposits as a possible future step.

Fines

Following the Human Environment and Transport Inspectorate’s (ILT) threat of fines this year, Verpact came up with additional incentives for consumers: a national sweepstakes with cash prizes for those returning their bottles and cans and even a lottery to encourage people to do so.

Verpact also added 2,500 more drop-off points this year, saying it expects to meet its legal requirement to have 5,400 new collection points in supermarkets and public places before the end of the year.

Verpact invested more than €220 million in the deposit system last year and paid €626 million to consumers who returned their recyclables. But by failing to hand in all their bottles and cans, Dutch consumers left €129 million unclaimed. That money goes back into the deposit system and is spent on items like new return machines.

The Netherlands has some 9,900 deposit-return points and 23,000 donation points.

And although coffee capsules are not part of the cash-back scheme, since January 1, 2026, consumers can return them – along with household aerosols (think deodorant or whipped cream cans) – in the PMD bins (plastic packaging, metal packaging, and drink cartons) due to an agreement between Verpact and the Coffee Capsule Recycling Association, reports NU.nl.

item.title: Home buyers file nearly 1,000 complaints over unfair bidding
item.description:
Home buyers file nearly 1,000 complaints over unfair bidding

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

House hunters in the Netherlands are still being pressured to raise their offers and kept in the dark about rival bids, according to almost 1,000 complaints logged since February by home owners’ association Vereniging Eigen Huis (VEH).

The association’s complaints hotline, which it reopened in February after a five-year gap, received 921 reports from buyers and sellers by early July, broadcaster NOS reported.

Buyers describe being pushed towards higher offers after being warned about competing bids that later could not be found in the official log, and winning bids being entered after the deadline or by the agent.

One buyer told NOS he was urged to add €10,000 to a €265,000 offer to secure a house, then found no higher bid recorded afterwards.

VEH says voluntary industry guidelines have failed to protect consumers. It found in May that most buyers experience unfair bidding. It wants the buying process written into law to improve transparency.

Buyers and sellers must be able to trust that the process is fair and verifiable, said VEH director Cindy Kremer, which is why statutory rules are needed “with supervision and enforcement, so breaches actually carry consequences”.

The government has promised action but not yet delivered anything concrete. Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan signalled in the spring that she would put regulatory options to parliament over the summer – plans which have yet to appear.

The estate agents’ associations are not resisting changes. The largest, NVM, said the reopened hotline could be useful but defended its own bidding protocol. Rival body Vastgoed Nederland said it was for the government to set firm rules.

PVV MP Jeremy Mooiman is drafting a private member’s bill to set a statutory standard for all agents.

item.title: Number of young people relying on benefits continues to rise
item.description:
Number of young people relying on benefits continues to rise

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of people claiming welfare benefits in the Netherlands has risen for the third year in a row, with the steepest increase among people under 27 years old, according to figures from national statistics agency CBS.

At the end of the second quarter of 2026, 413,000 people below the state pension age were receiving welfare, 4,000 more than a year earlier.

The total has now risen year-on-year for 12 consecutive quarters, though it remains slightly below its level before the coronavirus pandemic.

Sharpest rise among under-27s
Claims went up across all age groups, but fastest among the young. The number of under-27s on welfare rose 5.7% from a year earlier to 44,000, and has climbed by 27% since late 2022.

Among people aged 45 up to the state pension age, the number edged up 0.2% to 229,000, while 140,000 people aged 27 to 45 were claiming, a rise of 0.8%.
In the first quarter, more people started claiming welfare than left it – the 14th quarter in a row that arrivals rose faster than departures.

Welfare, which is administered by local councils, is paid to people of working age with no other income. The rise comes as unemployment has grown, reaching 4% earlier in the summer.

item.title: Dutch women beat Belgium to reach hockey World Cup final
item.description:
Dutch women beat Belgium to reach hockey World Cup final

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch women’s hockey team have reached their eighth World Cup final in a row, beating Belgium 1-0 in Amstelveen on Thursday, and are now one win from a fourth world title in succession – a feat no country has ever achieved.

The final is on Saturday at 18.00 at the Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen, against either Argentina or Australia.

Frédérique Matla scored the only goal in the first half against Belgium. In the second half, Belgium thought they had scored an equalising goal but it was disallowed due to a foul after a video review.

The Dutch were also briefly reduced to ten players after a yellow card.

Fourth title in sight

The Netherlands have won the last three World Cups, in 2014, 2018 and 2022, and no country has won the women’s title four times in succession. They reached the semi-finals with a 4-1 win over China on Sunday.

The Dutch men play their own semi-final later on Friday against Spain.
